concepts.label: Chess
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why checkmate ends play without capturing the king.
concepts.card: Chess ends in checkmate when the opposing king is attacked and no legal move can remove the threat. The king is never actually captured. A different ending, stalemate, occurs when a player has no legal move but their king is not attacked.
concepts.original_description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

evidence.note: Articles 1.4 and 5.2.1 support the objective, prohibition of king capture and contrasting stalemate condition; no claim that every immobile king is stalemated.

relations.note: The laws distinguish checkmate from stalemate through whether the immobile side's king is attacked.

imported_records.description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

concepts.label: Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect surrounding space with the capture of groups that lose every liberty.
concepts.card: Go players place stones on grid intersections to surround space. Connected stones share liberties: empty neighboring intersections along the grid lines. When an opponent occupies every liberty, the whole connected string is captured, linking local fights over stones with the larger struggle for territory.
concepts.original_description: Exploring territorial strategy and pattern recognition in the game of Go.

evidence.note: BGA introduction and capture paragraphs support intersections, orthogonal liberties and capture of a connected string; diagonal contact is not treated as connection.

relations.note: The teaching guide explains Go capture through the shared liberties of connected stones.

concepts.label: Shogi
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain the piece-reuse feature of shogi through a directly supported broad-game overview, leaving the perpetual-check exception to its separate rule card.
concepts.card: Shogi is Japanese chess with a distinctive form of piece reuse. Captured pieces become reserves for their captor. Instead of moving a piece already on the board, a player can spend a turn returning a captured piece to play on their own side.
concepts.original_description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

evidence.locator: PDF pages 1, 3 and 12, Comparisons and Placing Captured Pieces
evidence.note: Captured pieces become the captor’s reserves and may be returned to play instead of moving a board piece; no unrestricted-drop or automatic-promotion claim is used.

relations.note: The guide explicitly compares shogi with European chess and identifies returning captured pieces as a difference.

imported_records.description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

concepts.label: Backgammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect dice-limited movement with the race to remove all fifteen checkers.
concepts.card: Backgammon combines a race with obstacles. Each player moves fifteen checkers according to dice rolls, aiming to gather them in the home board and remove them. Landing on a lone opposing checker sends it to the bar, where it must re-enter before other checkers move.
concepts.original_description: Exploring strategic play involving movement, probability and dice.

evidence.locator: Object of the Game and Movement
evidence.note: USBGF Object, Movement and Hitting sections support fifteen checkers, dice movement, bearing-off objective and priority of bar entry; a hit requires landing on a lone checker.

relations.note: The rules make re-entry of hit checkers a compulsory interruption of normal checker movement.

imported_records.description: Exploring strategic play involving movement, probability and dice.

concepts.label: Othello
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a placement changes ownership of intervening discs.
concepts.card: Othello changes the ownership of pieces already on the board. A player places a disc to bracket an uninterrupted line of opposing discs, then flips those discs to their color. The winner has more discs when neither player can make a legal move.

evidence.note: Official outflanking and ending rules support placement, flipping and the final majority; the game need not fill all sixty-four squares.

relations.note: A lack of outflanking moves determines both forced passes and the eventual end of the game.

concepts.label: Contract bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how bidding fixes a partnership's trick-taking target before play.
concepts.card: In contract bridge, four players form two partnerships. Bidding establishes a contract specifying a number of tricks and a trump suit, or no trumps. During play, one partner's cards are exposed as dummy, and the declarer chooses cards from both partnership hands.
concepts.original_description: Exploring partnership bidding and trick-taking strategy.

evidence.note: ACBL Basics, Auction and Play support partnerships, contract denomination and dummy control; bidding numbers count tricks above the initial six, so the card avoids equating the printed bid with total tricks.

relations.note: ACBL's play explanation assigns the exposed partnership hand to declarer's decisions after the auction.

imported_records.description: Exploring partnership bidding and trick-taking strategy.

concepts.label: Senet
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect an Egyptian board race with New Kingdom beliefs about the afterlife.
concepts.card: Senet used a thirty-square board in ancient Egypt. Its imagery became more than decoration: during the New Kingdom, the game's passage through marked hazards was associated with the deceased person's journey toward the afterlife. Surviving game boxes connect recreation with funerary belief.

evidence.locator: Senet; Why is this game important?
evidence.note: The Met's Senet and importance sections support thirty squares, New Kingdom association and funerary objects; avoid presenting reconstructed detailed rules as certain.

relations.note: The museum documents double-sided game boxes carrying senet on one side and Twenty Squares on the other.

concepts.label: Twenty Squares
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how an imported ancient game acquired Egyptian markings and visual conventions.
concepts.card: Twenty Squares spread across the ancient Near East and was later imported into Egypt. Surviving boards reveal adaptation rather than simple copying: special squares on Near Eastern examples display rosettes, while Egyptian examples use hieroglyphs. A shared game could acquire a different visual language.

evidence.note: The Met explicitly reports geographic spread, import into Egypt and contrasting markings; no claim that all surviving boards preserve markings or identical rules.

relations.note: The museum describes Egyptian boxes accommodating both games, making their material comparison explicit.

concepts.label: Dick Fosbury
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine an athlete whose enduring influence came from a new jumping style.
concepts.card: Dick Fosbury's lasting influence came from the high-jump technique bearing his name. He won Olympic gold in 1968, but his legacy extended beyond that result: the Fosbury Flop transformed how the event was approached. Olympedia distinguishes this technical influence from his relatively brief competitive prominence.

evidence.note: Olympedia biography supports 1968 gold, technique and enduring influence; the card does not invent biomechanical details absent from this source.

relations.note: The biography identifies Fosbury's innovation and Olympic result specifically with the high-jump event.

concepts.label: James Naismith
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how indoor space and injury constraints shaped basketball's original design.
concepts.card: James Naismith devised basketball at Springfield in 1891 to provide an engaging indoor winter activity. Avoiding the rough collisions of outdoor games shaped the design. Elevated peach baskets required players to toss the ball toward a goal rather than charge through it.

evidence.locator: A New Game; The Birth of Basketball
evidence.note: Springfield's account supports the winter brief, concern about roughness, elevated baskets and tossing; it does not establish that every modern rule originated unchanged in 1891.

relations.note: The college's historical account identifies Naismith as basketball's inventor and explains the game's design constraints.

concepts.label: En passant
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand the pawn capture available only immediately after a neighboring two-square advance.
concepts.card: An en passant capture answers a pawn's two-square first advance. An opposing pawn beside its destination may capture it as though it had moved only one square. The opportunity exists only on the immediately following move; waiting forfeits this particular capture.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.7.3.1–2 supports neighboring same-rank pawns, the two-square advance and immediate-next-move limit; no other capture window is implied.

relations.note: FIDE defines en passant as a special pawn capture within the chess movement rules.

concepts.label: Castling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish permanent loss of castling rights from temporary obstacles.
concepts.card: Castling moves a king and rook in one turn, but permission depends on more than empty squares. Moving the king or the relevant rook permanently loses that castling right. Pieces between them or attacks on the king's starting, crossing or destination square can temporarily prevent it.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.8.2 distinguishes forfeited rights from temporary obstruction; the attacked-square restriction concerns the king's route, not every square the rook crosses.

relations.note: FIDE explicitly defines castling as a king-and-rook move within the chess movement rules.

concepts.label: Stalemate
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish having no legal move from being checkmated.
concepts.card: Stalemate is a drawn chess position in which the player to move has no legal move and their king is not in check. The distinction from checkmate is crucial: immobilizing the opponent does not win if no attack on the king accompanies that immobilization.

evidence.note: FIDE 5.2.1 supports side-to-move, absence of any legal move, no check and immediate draw; immobility of one piece alone is insufficient.

relations.note: The laws define stalemate as one of chess's game-ending draw conditions.

concepts.label: Dead position in chess
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a draw where neither side can ever deliver legal checkmate.
concepts.card: A dead position ends a chess game because neither player could checkmate through any possible sequence of legal moves. This is stronger than saying that checkmate seems unlikely or cannot be forced: even cooperative play by the opponent would not make mate possible.

evidence.note: FIDE 5.2.2 quantifies over any legal sequence; the cooperative-play explanation unpacks that condition rather than adding a material-count rule.

relations.note: Both end the game as a draw, but stalemate concerns present legal moves while dead position concerns impossibility of future mate.

concepts.label: Touch-move rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how deliberate touching commits a player when a legal move exists.
concepts.card: In over-the-board chess, deliberately touching one of your pieces with the intention of moving it normally commits you to move that piece if a legal move exists. Adjusting a piece after announcing that intention is different. Accidental contact is not treated as deliberate selection.

evidence.note: FIDE 4.2–4.5 support intentional contact, prior adjustment declaration and legal-move qualification; this describes own-piece handling rather than every multi-piece exception.

relations.note: FIDE's Act of Moving the Pieces regulates how a player's physical selection becomes binding.

concepts.label: Threefold repetition
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain the claimable three-occurrence draw procedure, including the timing of a claim before a qualifying intended move.
concepts.card: Under the cited FIDE rules, threefold repetition creates a claimable draw rather than automatically stopping play. A player whose turn it is may claim when the position has just appeared for the third time, or first record an intended move that will produce that recurrence.

evidence.note: FIDE 9.2.1–2 supports both current-position and intended-move claims by the player to move; the contrast with 9.6.1 avoids repeating only fivefold's position-identity lesson.

relations.note: The rules distinguish a player's threefold claim from the automatic fivefold repetition draw.

concepts.label: Underpromotion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that promotion may choose a rook, bishop or knight instead of queen.
concepts.card: A pawn reaching its final rank need not become a queen. Underpromotion chooses a rook, bishop or knight instead. The new piece takes effect immediately, and the available choices do not depend on which pieces were captured earlier in the game.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.7.3.3–5 support all alternatives, immediate effect and independence from captured pieces; no unsupported tactical claim explains why a particular choice wins.

relations.note: FIDE's pawn-promotion rule explicitly permits the three non-queen choices described here.

concepts.label: Liberties in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count shared adjacent empty points for an entire connected string.
concepts.card: A liberty is an empty intersection directly beside a Go stone along a horizontal or vertical line. Connected stones share their liberties as one string. Surrounding every liberty captures the entire string, so adding a connection can change the survival prospects of several stones at once.

evidence.note: BGA capture section supports orthogonal adjacency and whole-string treatment; the connection consequence follows directly from sharing the resulting string's liberties.

relations.note: The Go guide uses liberties to define when individual stones and connected strings are captured.

concepts.label: Eyes in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why two separate internal spaces protect a group from capture.
concepts.card: An eye is an internal space in a connected Go group. Two genuine, separate eyes can keep a group safe: an opponent cannot fill both in one move, and occupying the first would be self-capture rather than capturing the surrounding stones.

evidence.locator: Life and death and the concept of eyes
evidence.note: BGA Life and death and self-capture examples support two-eye safety; genuine eyes prevents confusing superficial holes with the protected spaces in the rule explanation.

relations.note: The guide explains eye-based survival through internal liberties and the prohibition on noncapturing self-capture.

concepts.label: Ko rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why immediate recapture must wait for a play elsewhere.
concepts.card: A ko capture can create an opportunity for immediate recapture that would restore the previous position. The basic ko rule forbids that immediate reply. The player must first play elsewhere, giving the opponent an opportunity to respond or end the local cycle.

evidence.note: BGA ko diagrams and explanatory paragraph support immediate-recapture restriction and intervening play; this does not claim that a single intervening move overrides every superko rule.
Superko forbids longer repeating positions; the comparison is editorial.

relations.note: Immediate ko and situational superko both limit repetition, but the latter also addresses longer cycles such as triple ko.

concepts.label: Seki
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize mutual survival when either attack would allow the opponent to capture.
concepts.card: Seki is mutual survival in Go without each group having two independent eyes. Neighboring groups share a shortage of liberties, and either player's attempt to capture can allow the opponent to capture first. Leaving the position alone therefore preserves both sides' stones.

evidence.locator: Seki: a kind of local stalemate
evidence.note: BGA's seki examples support mutual stand-off and shortage of liberties; no universal territory-scoring rule is added because rulesets differ.

relations.note: The guide introduces seki as an exception to the simple expectation that a group lacking two eyes will die.

concepts.label: Komi
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand points compensating White for playing second.
concepts.card: Komi compensates the player using White stones for Black's first move in Go. It adds points to White's final score rather than adding stones to the board. The British Go Association's cited default uses seven-and-a-half points; other rules or agreements can use different values.

evidence.note: BGA Default Rules gives 7½ and contrasts traditional Japanese values; How to Play explains compensation rather than placement of stones.
The guide explains compensation to White for Black moving first.

relations.note: The tournament rules identify komi as a score adjustment within Go, separately from handicap-stone placement.

concepts.label: Situational superko
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare a whole-game repetition ban with the immediate ko restriction.
concepts.card: Under the British Go Association's AGA-style rule, a player cannot make a play that recreates a board position previously created by that player. This reaches beyond immediate ko recapture, preventing longer repeating cycles such as triple ko from continuing indefinitely.

evidence.note: The precise BGA same-player formulation and triple-ko motivation are retained; this is not asserted to describe every international superko variant.

relations.note: BGA describes its superko restriction as preventing triple ko and other repeated positions beyond the basic local cycle.

concepts.label: Area and territory scoring in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare counting occupied points with counting territory plus prisoners.
concepts.card: Territory scoring counts enclosed empty points and captured stones; area scoring counts enclosed points and stones still occupying the board. That difference changes whether filling your own territory costs a point. AGA rules use pass stones to permit territory-style counting within an area-scoring framework.

evidence.note: BGA comparison explicitly supports both definitions, defensive-fill consequence and pass-stone accommodation; the card avoids claiming universal exact equality of final counts.

relations.note: The comparison identifies these as alternative Go scoring systems and explains their practical counting differences.

concepts.label: Doubling cube
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how accepting a double transfers the right to offer the next redouble.
concepts.card: Backgammon's doubling cube lets a player offer to raise the game's value before rolling. The opponent can decline and concede at the old value, or accept. Acceptance transfers ownership of the cube, so only that player may offer the next redouble.

evidence.note: USBGF Doubling supports timing, decline cost and ownership transfer; describe points rather than instructing anyone to gamble or implying tournament exceptions do not exist.

relations.note: The federation presents the cube as the game's mechanism for offering and accepting increased stakes.
